claim: Fgf4, 8, 9, and 17 are all expressed in the AER in vertebrates.
source: In vertebrates, Fgf 4, 8, 9, and 17 are all expressed in the AER.
evidence: This is stated as a general fact about vertebrate limb development in the abstract.

claim: Key Fgf ligands are expressed in the mesenchyme in the salamander (axolotl) developing and regenerating limb.
source: An exception to this paradigm is the salamander (axolotl) developing and regenerating limb, where key Fgf ligands are expressed in the mesenchyme.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known exception to the vertebrate paradigm.

claim: Mesenchymal expression of Amex.Fgf8 in axolotl has been suggested to be critical for regeneration.
source: The mesenchymal expression of Amex.Fgf8 in axolotl has been suggested to be critical for regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract referencing prior literature.

claim: A large body of mouse and chick studies have defined a set of transcription factors and canonical Wnt signaling as the main regulators of epidermal Fgf8 expression.
source: A large body of mouse and chick studies have defined a set of transcription factors and canonical Wnt signaling as the main regulators of epidermal Fgf8 expression in these organisms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Amex.Wnt3a is expressed in axolotl limb epidermis, similar to chicken and mouse.
source: We found that Amex.Wnt3a is expressed in axolotl limb epidermis, similar to chicken and mouse.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Unlike in amniotes, Wnt target genes are activated preferentially in limb mesenchyme rather than in epidermis in axolotl.
source: However, unlike in amniotes, Wnt target genes are activated preferentially in limb mesenchyme rather than in epidermis.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Inhibition of Wnt signaling results in downregulation of mesenchymal Amex.Fgf8 expression.
source: Inhibition and activation of Wnt signaling results in downregulation and upregulation of mesenchymal Amex.Fgf8 expression, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Activation of Wnt signaling results in upregulation of mesenchymal Amex.Fgf8 expression.
source: Inhibition and activation of Wnt signaling results in downregulation and upregulation of mesenchymal Amex.Fgf8 expression, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: A shift in tissue responsiveness to canonical Wnt signaling from epidermis to mesenchyme contributes to the unique mesenchymal Amex.Fgf8 expression in axolotl.
source: These results implicate a shift in tissue responsiveness to canonical Wnt signaling from epidermis to mesenchyme as one step contributing to the unique mesenchymal Amex.Fgf8 expression seen in the axolotl.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the experimental results.

claim: Fgf signaling is necessary for normal limb development and for limb regeneration in the axolotl.
source: Signaling mediated by members of the fibroblast growth factor (Fgf) family is necessary for normal limb development and for limb regeneration in the salamander Ambystoma mexicanum (axolotl), a primary model for regeneration research (Nacu et al., 2016; Purushothaman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Fgf signaling is required for limb development in mouse.
source: In less-regenerative tetrapods, like mouse (Mus musculus), Fgf signaling is similarly required for limb development (Lewandoski et al., 2000; Moon and Capecchi, 2000; Sun et al., 2002; Mariani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Fgfs 4, 8, 9, and 17 are produced by cells in the AER in mammals.
source: In mammals, Fgfs 4, 8, 9, and 17 are produced by cells in the Apical Ectodermal Ridge (AER), a thickened epidermal structure at the distal dorsoventral boundary of the limb bud.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Fgf signals from the AER act on the underlying mesenchyme to sustain its growth and patterning.
source: Fgf signals from the AER act on the underlying mesenchyme to sustain its growth and patterning.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Mmu.Fgf8 is the only AER Fgf that is individually required for normal limb development in mice.
source: Of the AER Fgfs, Mmu.Fgf8 is the only one that is individually required for normal limb development in mice (Mariani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: The axolotl limb blastema resembles the limb bud at both the morphological and transcriptional level.
source: Limb regeneration in the axolotl proceeds through the formation of the blastema, a structure that resembles the limb bud, both at the morphological and transcriptional level (Gerber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Amex.Fgfs 8, 9, and 17 are expressed in the mesenchymal compartment in both the axolotl limb blastema and limb bud.
source: In both the axolotl limb blastema and limb bud, Amex.Fgfs 8, 9, and 17 are expressed in the mesenchymal compartment, unlike in other vertebrates, while Amex.Fgf4 transcription is negligible or absent (Christensen et al., 2002; Nacu et al., 2016; Purushothaman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Amex.Fgf4 transcription is negligible or absent in the axolotl limb blastema and limb bud.
source: In both the axolotl limb blastema and limb bud, Amex.Fgfs 8, 9, and 17 are expressed in the mesenchymal compartment, unlike in other vertebrates, while Amex.Fgf4 transcription is negligible or absent (Christensen et al., 2002; Nacu et al., 2016; Purushothaman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Mesenchymal expression of Amex.Fgf8 is unique to the salamander limb.
source: Restriction of Amex.Fgf8 expression to the mesenchymal compartment is to our knowledge unique to the salamander limb, where it serves a crucial role in connecting positional identity with growth and patterning during limb regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the authors' assessment based on their knowledge.

claim: Amex.Fgf8 expression is restricted to the anterior mesenchyme of the regenerating blastema.
source: Nacu et al. showed that Amex.Fgf8 expression is restricted to the anterior mesenchyme of the regenerating blastema, while cells of the posterior blastema mesenchyme do not express Amex.Fgf8 (Nacu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Cells of the posterior blastema mesenchyme do not express Amex.Fgf8.
source: Nacu et al. showed that Amex.Fgf8 expression is restricted to the anterior mesenchyme of the regenerating blastema, while cells of the posterior blastema mesenchyme do not express Amex.Fgf8 (Nacu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Anterior cells express Amex.Fgf8 and posterior cells express Amex.Shh after limb amputation.
source: When a limb amputation is performed, anterior cells express Amex.Fgf8 and posterior cells express Amex.Shh, initiating a positive feedback loop in which Amex.Fgf8 and Amex.Shh reciprocally maintain each other's expression: prolonged expression of both signaling molecules sustains blastema growth and limb regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the regeneration process.

claim: Amex.Fgf8 and Amex.Shh reciprocally maintain each other's expression in a positive feedback loop.
source: When a limb amputation is performed, anterior cells express Amex.Fgf8 and posterior cells express Amex.Shh, initiating a positive feedback loop in which Amex.Fgf8 and Amex.Shh reciprocally maintain each other's expression: prolonged expression of both signaling molecules sustains blastema growth and limb regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the regeneration process.

claim: Prolonged expression of Amex.Fgf8 and Amex.Shh sustains blastema growth and limb regeneration.
source: When a limb amputation is performed, anterior cells express Amex.Fgf8 and posterior cells express Amex.Shh, initiating a positive feedback loop in which Amex.Fgf8 and Amex.Shh reciprocally maintain each other's expression: prolonged expression of both signaling molecules sustains blastema growth and limb regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the regeneration process.

claim: The positive feedback relationship between Fgfs and Shh was initially described in the mammalian limb, between Shh in the posterior mesenchyme and Fgf8 in the epidermis.
source: It is interesting to note that the positive feedback relationship between Fgfs and Shh was initially described in the mammalian limb, between Shh in the posterior mesenchyme and Fgf8 in the epidermis (Laufer et al., 1994; Niswander et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Expression of Mmu.Fgf8 in the mouse limb bud AER is controlled at the genetic level by a set of enhancers proximal to the gene locus.
source: In the mouse limb bud AER, expression of Mmu.Fgf8 is controlled at the genetic level by a set of enhancers proximal to the gene locus (Marinić et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Conserved orthologs of the majority of mouse Fgf8 enhancers are present in the axolotl genome.
source: Schlossnig et al. recently determined that conserved orthologs of the majority of these enhancers are present in the axolotl genome, and that at least one of these drives expression of a reporter construct in the mesenchyme of the axolotl limb (Schloissnig et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: At least one conserved Fgf8 enhancer drives expression of a reporter construct in the mesenchyme of the axolotl limb.
source: Schlossnig et al. recently determined that conserved orthologs of the majority of these enhancers are present in the axolotl genome, and that at least one of these drives expression of a reporter construct in the mesenchyme of the axolotl limb (Schloissnig et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Changes at the level of transacting factors may determine the divergent expression of Amex.Fgf8 in the axolotl limb.
source: This suggests that changes at the level of transacting factors may determine the divergent expression of Amex.Fgf8 in the axolotl limb.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from the cited work.

claim: AER expression of Mmu.Fgf8 in mice is dependent on mesenchymal Mmu.Fgf10 acting through the epidermis-specific receptor isoform Mmu.Fgfr2b.
source: In mice, AER expression of Mmu.Fgf8 has been shown to be dependent on mesenchymal Mmu.Fgf10 acting through the epidermis-specific receptor isoform Mmu.Fgfr2b (Xu et al., 1998; De Moerlooze et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2006; Sekine et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Gga.Fgf10 induces epidermal expression of the canonical Wnt ligand Gga.Wnt3a in chick.
source: Using the chick model, it was established that Gga.Fgf10 induces epidermal expression of the canonical Wnt ligand Gga.Wnt3a.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge from chick studies.

claim: Wnt3a (chick) and Wnt3 (mouse), together with BMPR1a-dependent signaling, activate canonical Wnt signaling within AER cells to induce Fgf8.
source: Wnt3a (chick) and Wnt3 (mouse), together with BMPR1a-dependent signaling, activate canonical Wnt signaling within AER cells to induce Fgf8 (Kengaku et al., 1998; Kawakami et al., 2001; Barrow et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Genetic removal of epidermal Mmu.Wnt3 or β-catenin is sufficient to abolish Mmu.Fgf8 expression in the mouse limb.
source: In mice, genetic removal of epidermal Mmu.Wnt3 or the canonical Wnt signaling effector β-catenin is sufficient to abolish Mmu.Fgf8 expression in the limb, while expression of a constitutively active β-catenin markedly expands the Mmu.Fgf8 expression domain and induces ectopic Mmu.Fgf8 expression in the dorsal and ventral epidermis (Barrow et al., 2003; Soshnikova et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Expression of a constitutively active β-catenin markedly expands the Mmu.Fgf8 expression domain and induces ectopic Mmu.Fgf8 expression in the dorsal and ventral epidermis in mouse.
source: In mice, genetic removal of epidermal Mmu.Wnt3 or the canonical Wnt signaling effector β-catenin is sufficient to abolish Mmu.Fgf8 expression in the limb, while expression of a constitutively active β-catenin markedly expands the Mmu.Fgf8 expression domain and induces ectopic Mmu.Fgf8 expression in the dorsal and ventral epidermis (Barrow et al., 2003; Soshnikova et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Mesenchymal expression of a constitutively active β-catenin construct appeared to potentially induce sporadic mesenchymal expression of Mmu.Fgf8 in mouse.
source: Furthermore, mesenchymal expression of a constitutively active β-catenin construct appeared to potentially induce sporadic mesenchymal expression of Mmu.Fgf8 (Hill et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Misexpression of β-catenin, Gga.Wnt3a or Gga.Lef1 is sufficient to induce Gga.Fgf8 expression ectopically in the dorsal and ventral epidermis in chick.
source: Similarly in the chick developing limb, misexpression of β-catenin, Gga.Wnt3a or the Wnt transcription factor Gga.Lef1 is sufficient to induce Gga.Fgf8 expression ectopically in the dorsal and ventral epidermis (Kengaku et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Buttonhead transcription factors Sp8 and Sp6 are necessary for Fgf8 expression and act downstream of canonical Wnt signaling in the mammalian limb.
source: In addition to Wnt signaling components, Buttonhead transcription factors Sp8 and Sp6 have also been shown to be necessary for Fgf8 expression and act downstream of canonical Wnt signaling in the mammalian limb (Kawakami et al., 2004; Talamillo et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2013; Haro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Dlx factors Dlx5 and Dlx6 are required to sustain Fgf8 expression, but are dispensable for its induction.
source: Finally, Dlx factors Dlx5 and Dlx6 have been implicated in the maintenance of the AER and are required to sustain Fgf8 expression, but are dispensable for its induction (Robledo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Amex.Fgf10 is expressed in the mesenchyme in the axolotl limb.
source: Amex.Fgf10 is expressed in the mesenchyme, along with Fgfs 8, 9, and 17 (Christensen et al., 2002; Nacu et al., 2016; Purushothaman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: No Fgf receptor is expressed in the axolotl epidermis according to a recent publication.
source: A recent publication reported that no Fgf receptor is expressed in the axolotl epidermis (Purushothaman et al., 2019), suggesting that the epidermal side of the interaction may be completely absent.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Fgfr2b expression is present in the basal epidermis of the newt blastema according to previous studies.
source: This is at odds with previous studies that showed Fgfr2b expression in the basal epidermis of the newt blastema (Poulin and Chiu, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Wnt3a expression is present in the salamander limb blastema as determined by qPCR.
source: The expression domain of Amex.Wnt3 ligands, the major Fgf8 AER regulators, has not been determined in the axolotl limb although Wnt3a expression is present in the salamander limb blastema as determined by qPCR (Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Amex.Wnt10 was found in similar amounts in lateral injuries and limb amputations, suggesting its role may be restricted to wound response.
source: Another canonical Wnt ligand, Amex.Wnt10 was found in similar amounts in lateral injuries (surface wounds that do not trigger regeneration) and limb amputations, suggesting its role may be restricted to wound response (Knapp et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Chemical activation of the canonical Wnt pathway increases cell proliferation in the salamander regenerating blastema.
source: Multiple studies reported that chemical activation of the canonical Wnt pathway increases cell proliferation in the salamander regenerating blastema (Singh et al., 2012; Wischin et al., 2017) but it has not been elucidated if the main site of canonical Wnt signaling activity is the blastema epidermis or mesenchyme.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Overexpression of the Wnt antagonist Axin1 is sufficient to block limb development and regeneration in the axolotl.
source: Although overexpression of the Wnt antagonist Axin1 is sufficient to block limb development and regeneration in the axolotl (Kawakami et al., 2006), it is unclear if this effect is mediated through downregulation of Amex.Fgf8.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: The epidermis of the axolotl blastema is necessary for both initial accumulation and proliferation of cells in the blastema.
source: Despite the expression of Fgf ligands in the mesenchymal compartment, classical experiments have shown that the epidermis of the axolotl blastema is necessary for both initial accumulation and proliferation of cells in the blastema (Thornton, 1957; Campbell and Crews, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Axolotl MARCKS like protein has been identified as an epidermal factor that induces the initial proliferation response in the blastema.
source: For example, Axolotl MARCKS like protein has been identified as an epidermal factor that induces the initial proliferation response in the blastema (Sugiura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Different cell populations are present in the regenerating axolotl epidermis.
source: Recent single-cell studies have highlighted that different cell populations are present in the regenerating axolotl epidermis (Leigh et al., 2018; Rodgers et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021), and previous studies have indicated that the basal layer of the axolotl epidermis expresses some markers of the mammalian AER, including Amex.Fibronectin1 and Amex.Dlx3 (Christensen and Tassava, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The basal layer of the axolotl epidermis expresses some markers of the mammalian AER, including Amex.Fibronectin1 and Amex.Dlx3.
source: Recent single-cell studies have highlighted that different cell populations are present in the regenerating axolotl epidermis (Leigh et al., 2018; Rodgers et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021), and previous studies have indicated that the basal layer of the axolotl epidermis expresses some markers of the mammalian AER, including Amex.Fibronectin1 and Amex.Dlx3 (Christensen and Tassava, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Amex.Sp6 is expressed in the epidermis of the axolotl limb bud and blastema.
source: Analysis of scRNA seq data from the axolotl limb bud and blastema (Li et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2021) revealed expression of Amex.Sp6 and Amex.Sp8 in the epidermis and not in mesenchyme (Figure 1A, A', B, B'). We performed whole-mount HCR staining in regenerating axolotl limb blastemas and limb buds (Figure 2B, B') and confirmed that Amex.Sp6 is expressed in the epidermis of the axolotl limb bud and regenerating blastema.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by scRNA-seq data and HCR staining.

claim: Amex.Sp6 is detected in the mesenchyme of the axolotl limb bud, in a domain proximal to Amex.Fgf8 expression.
source: Interestingly, we detected Amex.Sp6 also in the mesenchyme of the axolotl limb bud, in a domain proximal to Amex.Fgf8 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: Proximal mesenchymal expression of Amex.Sp6 was absent in the blastemas analyzed.
source: This proximal mesenchymal expression of Amex.Sp6 was absent in the blastemas that we analyzed and is unlikely to regulate the more distal Amex.Fgf8 expression in the axolotl limb bud.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: Amex.Sp8 is exclusively expressed in the epidermis with a strong enrichment in the basal layer in both the axolotl limb bud and blastema.
source: Using HCR in situ hybridization, we then found that Amex.Sp8 is exclusively expressed in the epidermis (Figure 2C, C'), with a strong enrichment in the basal layer (the inner layer facing the mesenchyme) in both the axolotl and limb bud and blastema.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: Buttonhead factors are unlikely to directly regulate Amex.Fgf8 expression in the mesenchyme.
source: This indicates that Buttonhead factors are unlikely to directly regulate Amex.Fgf8 expression in the mesenchyme and that the lack of Amex.Fgf8 expression in the axolotl epidermis is not due to the absence of these factors.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the expression data.

claim: The lack of Amex.Fgf8 expression in the axolotl epidermis is not due to the absence of Buttonhead factors.
source: This indicates that Buttonhead factors are unlikely to directly regulate Amex.Fgf8 expression in the mesenchyme and that the lack of Amex.Fgf8 expression in the axolotl epidermis is not due to the absence of these factors.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the expression data.

claim: Amex.Dlx5 expression is enriched in the distal mesenchyme and in the basal epidermis of the blastema and limb bud.
source: Whole-mount HCR staining revealed that expression of Amex.Dlx5 is enriched in the distal mesenchyme and in the basal epidermis of the blastema (Figure 2D) and limb bud (Figure 2D').
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: Expression of Amex.Dlx5 in the limb epidermis suggests that in the axolotl, similar to the mouse, Amex.Dlx5 is not sufficient to induce Amex.Fgf8 expression.
source: Expression of Amex.Dlx5 in the limb epidermis suggests that in the axolotl, similar to the mouse, Amex.Dlx5 is not sufficient to induce Amex.Fgf8 expression.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the expression data.

claim: The strong mesenchymal Amex.Dlx5 expression distinguishes the axolotl limb from the mammalian one and could be consistent with a conserved role in maintaining Amex.Fgf8 expression.
source: The strong mesenchymal Amex.Dlx5 expression distinguishes the axolotl limb from the mammalian one and could be consistent with a conserved role in maintaining Amex.Fgf8 expression.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the expression data.

claim: Amex.Lef1 is expressed broadly in the limb bud and blastema mesenchyme.
source: Using HCR, we found that Amex.Lef1 is expressed broadly in the limb bud and blastema mesenchyme (Figure 2E, E').
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: Amex.Lef1 expression is detected in the limb bud and blastema epidermis, strongest in the distal portion of the basal epidermis.
source: We also detected expression in the limb bud and blastema epidermis, strongest in the distal portion of the basal epidermis (Figure 2E, E').
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: At the levels observed, Amex.Lef1 is not sufficient to allow Amex.Fgf8 expression in the axolotl limb epidermis.
source: Considering that overexpression of Gga.Lef1 in chick is sufficient to induce ectopic Gga.Fgf8 expression (Kengaku et al., 1998), we note here that, at least at the levels observed, it is not sufficient to allow Amex.Fgf8 expression in the axolotl limb epidermis.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the expression data and comparison to chick.

claim: The broad expression pattern of Amex.Lef1 in the axolotl limb mesenchyme could be compatible with a role in inducing or maintaining mesenchymal Amex.Fgf8 expression in axolotl.
source: The broad expression pattern of Amex.Lef1 in the axolotl limb mesenchyme could be compatible with a role in inducing or maintaining mesenchymal Amex.Fgf8 expression in axolotl.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the expression data.

claim: The transcription factors Amex.Sp8, Amex.Sp6, Amex.Dlx5, Amex.Dlx6, and Amex.Lef1 are expressed in the axolotl developing and regenerating limb epidermis, in particular all are present in the basal epidermis.
source: Our analysis revealed that the transcription factors Amex.Sp8, Amex.Sp6, Amex.Dlx5, Amex.Dlx6, and Amex.Lef1 are expressed in the axolotl developing and regenerating limb epidermis, in particular all are present in the basal epidermis.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the Results section.

claim: In the axolotl limb epidermis, the combined endogenous expression of Amex.Sp8, Amex.Sp6, Amex.Dlx5, Amex.Dlx6, and Amex.Lef1 is not sufficient to activate Amex.Fgf8 transcription.
source: This indicates that, in the axolotl limb epidermis, the combined endogenous expression of these factors is not sufficient to activate Amex.Fgf8 transcription.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the expression data.

claim: Amex.Dlx5, Amex.Dlx6, and Amex.Lef1 are expressed in the limb bud and blastema mesenchyme, leaving open the possibility that they have a role in the regulation of Amex.Fgf8 expression in this tissue compartment.
source: While expression of Sp factors appeared uniquely epidermal, Amex.Dlx5, Amex.Dlx6, and Amex.Lef1 are expressed in the limb bud and blastema mesenchyme, leaving open the possibility that they have a role in the regulation of Amex.Fgf8 expression in this tissue compartment.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the expression data.

claim: Amex.Fgf10 transcripts are detected in the mesenchymal cluster in both blastema and limb bud scRNA seq datasets.
source: In both blastema and limb bud scRNA seq datasets, we detected Amex.Fgf10 transcripts in the mesenchymal cluster (Figure 3A, A'), consistent with previous reports (Christensen et al., 2002; Nacu et al., 2016; Purushothaman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by scRNA-seq data.

claim: HCR in situ hybridization confirmed strong and broad mesenchymal expression of Amex.Fgf10.
source: Using HCR in situ hybridization we confirmed strong and broad mesenchymal expression (Figure 4B, B').
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: Amex.Fgf10 transcripts are found in a small and distinct cell population located in the basal layer of the distal epidermis.
source: Surprisingly, we additionally found Amex.Fgf10 transcripts in a small and distinct cell population located in the basal layer of the distal epidermis.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: The Amex.Fgf10-expressing population in the basal epidermis is not of mesenchymal origin.
source: To exclude that this population is of mesenchymal origin we performed HCR in situ hybridization and lineage tracing using Prrx1-Cre transgenic axolotls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Gerber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Amex.Fgfr2b transcripts are detected through the entire basal epidermis of the blastema and limb bud.
source: In the axolotl, using HCR, we detected Amex.Fgfr2b transcripts through the entire basal epidermis of the blastema (Figure 4C) and limb bud (Figure 4C'), consistent with Amex.Fgf10 signaling to the epidermis as in other vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: Amex.Fgfr2b expression is consistent with Amex.Fgf10 signaling to the epidermis as in other vertebrates.
source: In the axolotl, using HCR, we detected Amex.Fgfr2b transcripts through the entire basal epidermis of the blastema (Figure 4C) and limb bud (Figure 4C'), consistent with Amex.Fgf10 signaling to the epidermis as in other vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the expression data.

claim: Amex.Wnt3a transcripts are found in the epidermal cluster in scRNA-seq data.
source: Fgf10 signaling is thought to be required for expression of Mmu.Wnt3 in mouse and Gga.Wnt3a in chick. We therefore assessed expression of both Amex.Wnt3 and Amex.Wnt3a: we found Amex.Wnt3a transcripts in the epidermal cluster (Figure 3B, B'), while we could only detect negligible Amex.Wnt3 transcripts in any cell type.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by scRNA-seq data.

claim: Only negligible Amex.Wnt3 transcripts are detected in any cell type in scRNA-seq data.
source: Fgf10 signaling is thought to be required for expression of Mmu.Wnt3 in mouse and Gga.Wnt3a in chick. We therefore assessed expression of both Amex.Wnt3 and Amex.Wnt3a: we found Amex.Wnt3a transcripts in the epidermal cluster (Figure 3B, B'), while we could only detect negligible Amex.Wnt3 transcripts in any cell type.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by scRNA-seq data.

claim: HCR data confirmed that Wnt3a expression is present in the axolotl limb bud and blastema basal epidermis.
source: HCR data confirmed that Wnt3a expression is present in the axolotl limb bud and blastema basal epidermis (Figure 4D, D').
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: The epidermal induction of Amex.Wnt3a is downstream of mesenchymal Amex.Fgf10 signaling in the axolotl limb as in mouse.
source: These results suggest that the epidermal induction of Amex.Wnt3a is downstream of mesenchymal Amex.Fgf10 signaling in the axolotl limb as in mouse.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the expression data.

claim: Amex.Axin2 expression in the axolotl limb is biased toward the mesenchymal compartment in single-cell analysis.
source: Single-cell analysis indicated that Amex.Axin2 expression in the axolotl limb is biased toward the mesenchymal compartment (Figure 3C, C').
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by scRNA-seq data.

claim: Whole-mount HCR confirmed strong Amex.Axin2 expression in the mesenchyme, with a distal and subepidermal enrichment in both the axolotl blastema and limb bud.
source: Using whole-mount HCR, we confirmed strong expression in the mesenchyme, with a distal and subepidermal enrichment in both the axolotl blastema (Figure 4D, E) and limb bud (Figure 4D', E').
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: Epidermal Amex.Axin2 expression is present, but weaker than mesenchymal expression.
source: Epidermal expression is also present, but weaker.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: The mesenchymal enrichment in Amex.Axin2 expression distinguishes the axolotl limb from the mammalian one.
source: The mesenchymal enrichment in Amex.Axin2 expression distinguishes the axolotl limb from the mammalian one.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the expression data.

claim: Amex.Rspo2 expression is absent from the axolotl developing and regenerating limb epidermis but present in the mesenchyme in single-cell analysis.
source: Our single-cell analysis revealed that Amex.Rspo2 expression is absent from the axolotl developing and regenerating limb epidermis but present in the mesenchyme (Figure 3D, D').
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by scRNA-seq data.

claim: HCR confirmed the strictly mesenchymal expression of Amex.Rspo2.
source: We confirmed the strictly mesenchymal expression of Amex.Rspo2 using HCR (Figure 4E, E').
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: Mesenchymal Amex.Rspo2 expression is biased along the dorsoventral axis in both the axolotl limb bud and blastema.
source: In both the axolotl limb bud and blastema, mesenchymal Amex.Rspo2 expression is biased along the dorsoventral axis, suggesting a possible role in dorsoventral limb patterning (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by HCR staining.

claim: IWR treatment induced a similar decrease in Amex.Axin2 and Amex.Fgf8 transcripts when compared to DMSO treated controls.
source: IWR treatment induced a similar decrease in Amex.Axin2 and Amex.Fgf8 transcripts when compared to Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) treated controls (Figure 5A, B), suggesting that canonical Wnt signaling is required to sustain expression of Amex.Fgf8 in the axolotl blastema mesenchyme.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by drug treatment experiments and quantification.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling is required to sustain expression of Amex.Fgf8 in the axolotl blastema mesenchyme.
source: IWR treatment induced a similar decrease in Amex.Axin2 and Amex.Fgf8 transcripts when compared to Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) treated controls (Figure 5A, B), suggesting that canonical Wnt signaling is required to sustain expression of Amex.Fgf8 in the axolotl blastema mesenchyme.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the drug treatment data.

claim: Amex.Axin2 expression was upregulated in all CHIR treatment conditions compared to controls.
source: As expected, Amex.Axin2 expression was upregulated in all CHIR treatment conditions compared to controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by drug treatment experiments and quantification.

claim: After 3 hr of CHIR treatment, expression of Amex.Fgf8 was significantly upregulated.
source: After 3 hr of CHIR treatment, expression of Amex.Fgf8 was significantly upregulated (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by drug treatment experiments and quantification.

claim: By 6 hr of CHIR treatment, Amex.Fgf8 was not significantly different in CHIR-treated and -untreated samples.
source: By 6 hr, we found that Amex.Fgf8 was not significantly different in CHIR-treated and -untreated samples while after 12-hr Amex.Fgf8 expression levels were significantly decreased when compared to control samples (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by drug treatment experiments and quantification.

claim: After 12 hr of CHIR treatment, Amex.Fgf8 expression levels were significantly decreased when compared to control samples.
source: By 6 hr, we found that Amex.Fgf8 was not significantly different in CHIR-treated and -untreated samples while after 12-hr Amex.Fgf8 expression levels were significantly decreased when compared to control samples (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by drug treatment experiments and quantification.

claim: Amex.Fgf8 transcripts, although upregulated after 3 hr of CHIR treatment, were always present exclusively in the native Amex.Fgf8 domain in the anterior blastema mesenchyme.
source: Amex.Fgf8 transcripts, although upregulated after 3 hr of CHIR treatment, were always present exclusively in the native Amex.Fgf8 domain in the anterior blastema mesenchyme (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by drug treatment experiments and imaging.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling regulates Amex.Fgf8 expression in the anterior mesenchyme.
source: Our results are consistent with canonical Wnt signaling regulating Amex.Fgf8 expression in the anterior mesenchyme.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the drug treatment data.

claim: Wnt activation is not sufficient to induce ectopic Amex.Fgf8 expression in the posterior mesenchyme nor in the epidermis.
source: Interestingly, while we observe a Wnt-induced upregulation of Amex.Fgf8 in the anterior mesenchyme, Wnt activation is not sufficient to induce ectopic Amex.Fgf8 expression in the posterior mesenchyme nor in the epidermis indicating regulation of Amex.Fgf8 by other, yet unidentified factors.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by drug treatment experiments and imaging.

claim: Regulation of Amex.Fgf8 involves other, yet unidentified factors.
source: Interestingly, while we observe a Wnt-induced upregulation of Amex.Fgf8 in the anterior mesenchyme, Wnt activation is not sufficient to induce ectopic Amex.Fgf8 expression in the posterior mesenchyme nor in the epidermis indicating regulation of Amex.Fgf8 by other, yet unidentified factors.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the drug treatment data.

claim: In all CHIR treatment conditions Amex.Axin2 expression retained a strong mesenchymal bias.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that in all treatment conditions Amex.Axin2 expression retained a strong mesenchymal bias, suggesting that the axolotl epidermis may be partially refractory to canonical Wnt signaling activation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by drug treatment experiments and imaging.

claim: The axolotl epidermis may be partially refractory to canonical Wnt signaling activation.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that in all treatment conditions Amex.Axin2 expression retained a strong mesenchymal bias, suggesting that the axolotl epidermis may be partially refractory to canonical Wnt signaling activation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on the drug treatment data.

claim: Upregulation of Amex.Axin2 after CHIR treatment is present in both mesenchymal and epidermal compartments, but stronger in the mesenchyme.
source: To verify this, we quantified the increase in Amex.Axin2 in the mesenchymal and epidermal compartments after 3 and 6 hr of CHIR treatment and found that upregulation of Amex.Axin2 is present in both compartments, but stronger in the mesenchyme (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section, supported by drug treatment experiments and quantification.

claim: Mesenchymal Axin2 increases 2.6-fold after 3 hr of CHIR treatment.
source: Mesenchymal Axin2 increases 2.6-fold after 3 hr and 4.4-fold after 6 hr of treatment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E with quantification data.

claim: Mesenchymal Axin2 increases 4.4-fold after 6 hr of CHIR treatment.
source: Mesenchymal Axin2 increases 2.6-fold after 3 hr and 4.4-fold after 6 hr of treatment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E with quantification data.

claim: Epidermal Axin2 increases 1.8-fold after 3 hr of CHIR treatment.
source: Epidermal Axin2 increases 1.8-fold after 3 hr and 1.7-fold after 6 hrs of treatment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E with quantification data.

claim: Epidermal Axin2 increases 1.7-fold after 6 hr of CHIR treatment.
source: Epidermal Axin2 increases 1.8-fold after 3 hr and 1.7-fold after 6 hrs of treatment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E with quantification data.

claim: The digital elements in salamander limbs are formed in an anterior to posterior order, contrary to other species.
source: The digital elements are formed in an anterior to posterior order, contrary to other species (Nye et al., 2003; Fröbisch et al., 2015; Purushothaman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Most of the components that act upstream of mammalian Fgf8 expression in the AER are present in the axolotl epidermis, with an enrichment in the most basal layer.
source: We found that most of the components that act upstream of mammalian Fgf8 expression in the AER are present in the axolotl epidermis, with an enrichment in the most basal layer.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the Discussion.

claim: Expression of Amex.Fgfr2b, Amex.Wnt3a, and the transcription factors Amex.Sp8, Amex.Sp6, Amex.Dlx5, Amex.Dlx6, and Amex.Lef1 in the axolotl epidermis is evidently insufficient to induce expression of Amex.Fgf8 in epidermis.
source: Expression of these components in the axolotl epidermis is evidently insufficient to induce expression of Amex.Fgf8 in epidermis.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion based on the expression data.

claim: Epidermal expression of Amex.Fgfr2b and Amex.Wnt3a suggests that in the axolotl limb, like in the mouse and chick limb, Amex.Fgf10 signals to the epidermis to induce the expression of a canonical Wnt3 ligand.
source: Epidermal expression of Amex.Fgfr2b and Amex.Wnt3a suggests that in the axolotl limb, like in the mouse and chick limb, Amex.Fgf10 signals to the epidermis to induce the expression of a canonical Wnt3 ligand.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion based on the expression data.

claim: In chick Gga.Wnt3a expression is restricted to the AER.
source: There are slight differences in the epidermal pattern of expression of Wnt3 ligands between the chick and mouse limb: in chick Gga.Wnt3a expression is restricted to the AER (Kawakami et al., 2001), while in mouse Mmu.Wnt3 expression is present in the entire limb epidermis (Barrow et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: In mouse Mmu.Wnt3 expression is present in the entire limb epidermis.
source: There are slight differences in the epidermal pattern of expression of Wnt3 ligands between the chick and mouse limb: in chick Gga.Wnt3a expression is restricted to the AER (Kawakami et al., 2001), while in mouse Mmu.Wnt3 expression is present in the entire limb epidermis (Barrow et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: It has been speculated that in both chick and mouse, Mmu.Wnt3/Gga.Wnt3a ligands signal to induce strong Wnt signaling activation specifically in the AER, a cell type that has an enhanced sensitivity to canonical Wnt signaling.
source: Nevertheless, it has been speculated that in both species, Mmu.Wnt3/Gga.Wnt3a ligands signal to induce strong Wnt signaling activation specifically in the AER, a cell type that has an enhanced sensitivity to canonical Wnt signaling (Kengaku et al., 1998; Barrow et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to supporting literature.

claim: In the axolotl, unlike the mouse, a discrete epidermal compartment exhibiting high activity of the canonical Wnt pathway is absent.
source: In the axolotl, unlike the mouse, we found that a discrete epidermal compartment exhibiting high activity of the canonical Wnt pathway is absent, while strong canonical Wnt pathway activity appears to be present in the mesenchyme.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the Discussion.

claim: Strong canonical Wnt pathway activity appears to be present in the mesenchyme in axolotl.
source: In the axolotl, unlike the mouse, we found that a discrete epidermal compartment exhibiting high activity of the canonical Wnt pathway is absent, while strong canonical Wnt pathway activity appears to be present in the mesenchyme.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the Discussion.

claim: The axolotl has lost competency to activate strong canonical Wnt signaling in the epidermis and diverted this competence to the mesenchyme.
source: Our data suggest that the axolotl has lost competency to activate strong canonical Wnt signaling in the epidermis and diverted this competence to the mesenchyme.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion based on the data.

claim: Rspondin2, a potentiator of Wnt signaling in the mouse epidermis is expressed strictly in the mesenchyme in axolotl.
source: Interestingly, Rspondin2, a potentiator of Wnt signaling in the mouse epidermis is expressed strictly in the mesenchyme in axolotl.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the Discussion.

claim: Pharmacological activation and inhibition of the Wnt pathway yielded results consistent with a role of Wnt signaling in promoting mesenchymal Amex.Fgf8 expression.
source: Pharmacological activation and inhibition of the Wnt pathway yielded results consistent with a role of Wnt signaling in promoting mesenchymal Amex.Fgf8 expression.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the Discussion.

claim: A positive effect of CHIR treatment on Amex.Fgf8 expression was present after 3 hr of treatment but disappeared when the perturbation was performed for longer durations, possibly due to indirect effects or negative feedbacks triggered by the ubiquitously high Wnt signaling environment.
source: A positive effect of CHIR treatment on Amex.Fgf8 expression was present after 3 hr of treatment but disappeared when the perturbation was performed for longer durations, possibly due to indirect effects or negative feedbacks triggered by the ubiquitously high Wnt signaling environment.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion based on the drug treatment data.

claim: The positive upstream regulatory role of Wnt signaling on Fgf8 is similar to that seen in chicken and mammals yet occurring in a different tissue compartment.
source: The positive upstream regulatory role of Wnt signaling is similar to that seen in chicken and mammals yet occurring in a different tissue compartment (Barrow et al., 2003; Soshnikova et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion based on the data and comparison to other species.

claim: The experiments have been performed at stages of limb development and regeneration subsequent to the initiation of Amex.Fgf8 expression and therefore indicate a function of canonical Wnt signaling at least in maintaining Amex.Fgf8 expression.
source: Our experiments have been performed at stages of limb development and regeneration subsequent to the initiation of Amex.Fgf8 expression and therefore indicate a function of canonical Wnt signaling at least in maintaining Amex.Fgf8 expression.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion based on the experimental design.

claim: In mouse and chick, canonical Wnt signaling is required for both the initiation and maintenance of endogenous Fgf8 expression.
source: In mouse and chick, canonical Wnt signaling is required for both the initiation and maintenance of endogenous Fgf8 expression and, when activated ectopically, can induce ectopic epidermal Fgf8 expression (Kengaku et al., 1998; Galceran et al., 1999; Barrow et al., 2003; Soshnikova et al., 2003; Kawakami et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to supporting literature.

claim: When canonical Wnt signaling is activated ectopically in mouse and chick, it can induce ectopic epidermal Fgf8 expression.
source: In mouse and chick, canonical Wnt signaling is required for both the initiation and maintenance of endogenous Fgf8 expression and, when activated ectopically, can induce ectopic epidermal Fgf8 expression (Kengaku et al., 1998; Galceran et al., 1999; Barrow et al., 2003; Soshnikova et al., 2003; Kawakami et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to supporting literature.

claim: In the axolotl, canonical Wnt activation was not sufficient to induce ectopic Amex.Fgf8 expression in the ectoderm.
source: Interestingly, in the axolotl, canonical Wnt activation was not sufficient to induce ectopic Amex.Fgf8 expression in the ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the Discussion.

claim: Classical mouse and chick studies have not fully clarified if the Wnt-dependent induction of ectopic Fgf8 expression is a direct and cell autonomous phenomenon.
source: Classical mouse and chick studies have not fully clarified if the Wnt-dependent induction of ectopic Fgf8 expression is a direct and cell autonomous phenomenon.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the Discussion about the literature.

claim: Ectopic Fgf8-expressing cells were often generated in stripes in mouse and chick studies, suggesting that Wnt signaling may act to induce a local tissue reorganization that is likely dependent on additional signaling components.
source: Ectopic Fgf8-expressing cells were often generated in stripes, suggesting that Wnt signaling may act to induce a local tissue reorganization that is likely dependent on additional signaling components, leaving open the possibility that β-catenin pathway activation may not be sufficient to induce Fgf8 expression cell autonomously in the mammalian and avian limb (Kengaku et al., 1998; Barrow et al., 2003; Soshnikova et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion based on observations from the literature.

claim: Amex.Lef1, Amex.Dlx5, and Amex.Dlx6 were expressed also in the axolotl mesenchyme, where they may play a role in inducing or sustaining Amex.Fgf8 expression.
source: Of the transcription factors that have been implicated in the regulation of AER Fgf8 expression, Amex.Lef1, Amex.Dlx5, and Amex.Dlx6 were expressed also in the axolotl mesenchyme, where they may play a role in inducing or sustaining Amex.Fgf8 expression.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion based on the expression data.

claim: The broad expression pattern of Amex.Lef1, Amex.Dlx5, and Amex.Dlx6 includes portions of the limb mesenchyme devoid of Amex.Fgf8 transcripts, suggesting they are not sufficient to induce Amex.Fgf8 expression outside of its native domain.
source: Nevertheless, their broad expression pattern includes portions of the limb mesenchyme devoid of Amex.Fgf8 transcripts, suggesting they are not sufficient to induce Amex.Fgf8 expression outside of its native domain.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion based on the expression data.

claim: Amex.Fgf10 expression is present not only in the axolotl limb mesenchyme but also in a small cell population localized in the basal layer of the limb bud and blastema epidermis.
source: In our study, we also report that Amex.Fgf10 expression is present not only in the axolotl limb mesenchyme but also in a small cell population localized in the basal layer of the limb bud and blastema epidermis.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the Discussion.

claim: The additional Amex.Fgf10 expression domain in the basal epidermis is to our knowledge unique to the axolotl.
source: This additional expression domain is to our knowledge unique to the axolotl; Fgf10 is considered a mesenchymal specific ligand, and the mesenchymal to epidermal Fgf10–Fgfr2b signaling interaction is conserved in the development of different organs across species, likely including the axolotl limb (Itoh, 2016) (and this study).
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the Discussion based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Fgf10 is considered a mesenchymal specific ligand.
source: This additional expression domain is to our knowledge unique to the axolotl; Fgf10 is considered a mesenchymal specific ligand, and the mesenchymal to epidermal Fgf10–Fgfr2b signaling interaction is conserved in the development of different organs across species, likely including the axolotl limb (Itoh, 2016) (and this study).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The mesenchymal to epidermal Fgf10–Fgfr2b signaling interaction is conserved in the development of different organs across species, likely including the axolotl limb.
source: This additional expression domain is to our knowledge unique to the axolotl; Fgf10 is considered a mesenchymal specific ligand, and the mesenchymal to epidermal Fgf10–Fgfr2b signaling interaction is conserved in the development of different organs across species, likely including the axolotl limb (Itoh, 2016) (and this study).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation and reference to the current study.

claim: The additional Amex.Fgf10-expressing population in the axolotl limb does not express the mesenchymal marker Amex.Prrx1.
source: We show that the additional Amex.Fgf10-expressing population in the axolotl limb is not derived from the blastema mesenchyme and does not express the mesenchymal marker Amex.Prrx1.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the Discussion.

claim: The additional Amex.Fgf10-expressing population in the axolotl limb is not derived from the blastema mesenchyme.
source: We show that the additional Amex.Fgf10-expressing population in the axolotl limb is not derived from the blastema mesenchyme and does not express the mesenchymal marker Amex.Prrx1.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the Discussion.

claim: Mesodermal cells of somitic origin are present in the zebrafish pectoral fin AER.
source: Interestingly, Masselink et al. showed that mesodermal cells of somitic origin are present in the zebrafish pectoral fin AER and that ablation of this cell population expands the Dre.Fgf8 expression domain in the fin ectoderm (Masselink et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Ablation of the somitic mesoderm-derived cell population in zebrafish expands the Dre.Fgf8 expression domain in the fin ectoderm.
source: Interestingly, Masselink et al. showed that mesodermal cells of somitic origin are present in the zebrafish pectoral fin AER and that ablation of this cell population expands the Dre.Fgf8 expression domain in the fin ectoderm (Masselink et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Loss of the somitic mesoderm-derived cell population in the tetrapod limb has been speculated to be necessary for temporal expansion of Fgf8 AER expression and fin to limb transition.
source: Loss of this somitic mesoderm-derived cell population in the tetrapod limb has been speculated to be necessary for temporal expansion of Fgf8 AER expression and fin to limb transition (Thorogood, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to supporting literature.

claim: Some of the adaptations of the axolotl limb patterning system may be important to accommodate specific requirements of limb regeneration.
source: Some of the adaptations of the axolotl limb patterning system may be important to accommodate specific requirements of limb regeneration, while features that are conserved across species may represent necessary elements of limb development.
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the Discussion.

claim: Features that are conserved across species may represent necessary elements of limb development.
source: Some of the adaptations of the axolotl limb patterning system may be important to accommodate specific requirements of limb regeneration, while features that are conserved across species may represent necessary elements of limb development.
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the Discussion.

claim: Mesenchymal expression of Amex.Fgf8 has been implicated in anterior–posterior patterning and in the intercalation capability in limb regeneration.
source: Mesenchymal expression of Amex.Fgf8 is of particular interest as it has been implicated in anterior–posterior patterning and in the intercalation capability in limb regeneration (Shimizu-Nishikawa et al., 2003; Makanae and Satoh, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Known regulators of AER Fgf8 expression are present in the axolotl epidermis, where they are not sufficient to induce Amex.Fgf8 expression.
source: Our study highlights that known regulators of AER Fgf8 expression are present in the axolotl epidermis, where they are not sufficient to induce Amex.Fgf8 expression and suggests that an epidermal to mesenchymal trade in sensitivity to canonical Wnt signaling may be an important factor for mesenchymal expression of Amex.Fgf8 and a unique feature of limb development and regeneration in the axolotl or salamanders in general.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: An epidermal to mesenchymal trade in sensitivity to canonical Wnt signaling may be an important factor for mesenchymal expression of Amex.Fgf8 and a unique feature of limb development and regeneration in the axolotl or salamanders in general.
source: Our study highlights that known regulators of AER Fgf8 expression are present in the axolotl epidermis, where they are not sufficient to induce Amex.Fgf8 expression and suggests that an epidermal to mesenchymal trade in sensitivity to canonical Wnt signaling may be an important factor for mesenchymal expression of Amex.Fgf8 and a unique feature of limb development and regeneration in the axolotl or salamanders in general.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion in the Discussion.
